They argue that the low-order approximations used by MI-based methods require two conditional-independence assumptions: the selected features must be independent given a candidate feature, and also independent given that candidate feature **and** the class label [4]. These assumptions correspond to making the two entropy decompositions exact [4].

However, conditioning on the label can create or reveal dependencies among the features. Thus, if the second assumption holds, the first generally cannot also hold, except under a very specific and unrealistic data-generating structure [7][8]. Moreover, in that exceptional structure, the candidate feature would be more informative about the label than the already selected feature group, so it should have been selected earlier—contradicting the feature-selection process [7].

In the Pairwise Q-distribution, the conditional for the newly ordered feature is constructed as the geometric mean of its pairwise conditionals with the previously selected features:

\[
q(x_{f_t}\mid x_{f_{<t}},y)
=
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{t-1}p(x_{f_t}\mid x_{f_i},y)\right)^{1/(t-1)}.
\]

This is a pairwise-based alternative that is more general than the Naive Bayes distribution [6]. The construction is tractable within the autoregressive decomposition, provided the conditional is tractable [7], and it can be updated recursively when a new feature is added [5]. The authors therefore justify it as both computationally convenient for forward feature selection and capable of going beyond the Naive Bayes assumption [6][7].

\[
p(X_{S_i}\mid X_i)=\prod_{j\in S_i}p(X_j\mid X_i),\qquad
p(X_{S_i}\mid X_i,Y)=\prod_{j\in S_i}p(X_j\mid X_i,Y).

[8]

Under this assumption, the subset–class mutual information decomposes into pairwise conditional mutual-information terms:
\[
I(X_{S_i\cup\{i\}};Y)
=
I(X_i;Y)+\sum_{j\in S_i} I(X_j;Y\mid X_i),
\]
i.e., terms involving only two features and the class label at a time. [3][8]

question_answers.operator-001:
Filter methods select variables independently of the forecasting or mining algorithm, typically by ranking their predictive strength and removing those below a threshold before prediction [3][4][7][8]. Their results can therefore be used with different algorithms and are relatively simple to understand [6].

Wrapper methods, by contrast, use the forecasting algorithm as a black-box evaluator and search for the feature subset that maximizes that algorithm’s performance, while accounting for feature dependencies [1][6][8]. They can yield better performance because they are tailored to the chosen algorithm, but are slower and less transferable to other algorithms [1][2].

It starts with no selected variables and picks the first variable having the highest mutual information with the target—i.e., the highest relevance [8][5].  

After that, it adds variables sequentially. At each step, among the unselected variables it chooses the one maximizing

\[
\text{relevance to the target} - \text{average redundancy with the already selected variables},

The Randomized Dependence Coefficient (RDC) measures dependence by taking the maximum correlation between randomized nonlinear copula projections of the two variables. Specifically, for samples \(X\) and \(Y\), it is defined as

\[
\operatorname{rdc}(X,Y;k,s)
=
\sup_{\alpha,\beta}
\rho\!\left(
\alpha^{T}\Phi_{k,s}(X),
\beta^{T}\Phi_{k,s}(Y)
\right),
\]

where \(k\) and \(s\) control the randomized feature mappings. [3][4] It is therefore a finite-dimensional estimator inspired by the HGR maximum correlation coefficient. [1][7]

For variables of dimensions \(p\) and \(q\) with \(n\) samples, its computational cost is \(O((p+q)^2 n)\), so it is linear in the sample size \(n\) when \(p\) and \(q\) are fixed. [3][4]
question_answers.operator-014:
RDC uses the empirical copula transformation to remove the effects of the variables’ marginal distributions—such as shifts, rescalings, and other monotonically increasing transformations—while preserving their dependence structure. [8] This makes RDC invariant to monotonic transformations and suitable for variables of arbitrary dimension. [2][7]

After transforming each variable to its empirical copula representation, RDC applies random nonlinear projections and computes the largest canonical correlation between the projected variables. [3][6] Thus, it focuses on the dependence relationship itself rather than on arbitrary scales or marginal distributions in the raw samples.

In mRMR, for a candidate feature \(X_i\), relevance is its mutual information with the class/target \(Y\), while redundancy is its average mutual information with the already selected features \(S\) [7].

- **MID (Mutual Information Difference):**
  \[
  f_{\mathrm{MID}}(X_i)
  = I(Y;X_i)-\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{X_s\in S} I(X_s;X_i)
  \]
  It maximizes relevance minus redundancy [7].

- **MIQ (Mutual Information Quotient):**
  \[
  f_{\mathrm{MIQ}}(X_i)
  =\frac{I(Y;X_i)}
  {\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{X_s\in S} I(X_s;X_i)}
  \]
  It maximizes the ratio of relevance to redundancy [7].

Thus, **MID combines relevance and redundancy by subtraction**, whereas **MIQ combines them by division** [7].

The authors chose the arithmetic mean because it preserves information from **all time points** while still capturing genes whose group differences are large only during a short portion of the experiment. Median and geometric mean could miss such transient patterns, whereas the maximum would rely on only one time point and ignore the rest [4][6][8]. Although the mean is affected by small F-statistics at time points without differences, it can still yield a substantial overall relevance value when some time points show strong differences [8].

They also tested multilayer aggregation (MLA), which combines the arithmetic mean, geometric mean, and median. However, it did not significantly improve the results and reduced the robustness of the feature-selection methods, so they selected the arithmetic mean as the most appropriate operator [5][7].

Without normalization, two similarly fluctuating signals—such as one ranging from 5–10 and another from 30–40—could appear dissimilar because of their different scales [1]. Z-score normalization centers each series around zero and removes amplitude differences, leaving primarily the shape, which is the aspect relevant for measuring redundancy with DTW [6]. It is therefore performed before constructing the DTW distance matrix [8].

Fast-mRMR applies several optimizations to original mRMR:

- **Greedy feature selection:** it uses the number of features to select to limit the number of feature comparisons, turning the quadratic process into a more efficient greedy one [4][8].
- **Caching:** mutual-information-related values are calculated once at the beginning and cached for reuse in later iterations, avoiding repeated calculations [5].
- **A new data-access pattern:** it redesigns how the input data are accessed to improve performance, especially for MI computations [5][7][8].

For the data-access optimization, the original mRMR access pattern is **featurewise**, whereas many algorithms use **rowwise** access. Fast-mRMR changes the storage/access arrangement so features can be accessed contiguously in a featurewise manner rather than requiring costly random access; this is particularly important on GPUs [5].

question_answers.operator-032:
MRmMC measures a candidate feature’s redundancy as its **average dependence—interpreted as multicollinearity—with the features already selected**. The candidate is evaluated by considering what happens when it is added to the current subset [2]. The resulting selection score subtracts this redundancy from the candidate’s relevance [4].

In practice, the redundancy is computed by:

1. Computing the mutual information between the candidate \(f_c\) and each selected feature \(f_s\) [4].
2. Summing those pairwise values.
3. Dividing the sum by the number of selected features:

\[
\operatorname{Red}(f_c,S)
=
\frac{\sum_{f_s\in S} I(f_c;f_s)}{|S|}.
\]

This is the same average-pairwise-MI form used to quantify redundancy against an already selected set [8]. The implementation therefore calculates `calculatedRedundancy[fc] / selectedFeatures.size()` and then uses

\[
\text{MRmMC}(f_c)=\text{relevance}(f_c)-\text{redundancy}(f_c).
\]

The measure is intended mainly for quantitative features and can capture both linear and nonlinear relationships [5].

The **Randomized Dependence Coefficient (RDC)** is a lightweight, finite-dimensional estimator of nonlinear dependence, designed in the spirit of the Hirschfeld–Gebelein–Rényi (HGR) maximum correlation coefficient because HGR is computationally intractable [1][5].

Given samples \(X\) and \(Y\), RDC computes

\[
\operatorname{rdc}(X,Y;k,s)
=
\sup_{\alpha,\beta}
\rho\!\left(
\alpha^\top \Phi(P(X);k,s),
\beta^\top \Phi(P(Y);k,s)
\right),
\]

where \(\rho\) is correlation [2]. Thus, it actually computes the **maximum correlation—equivalently, the first canonical correlation—between linear combinations of randomized nonlinear copula-feature projections of the two variables** [2][7]. It is therefore an estimator of HGR-style maximal nonlinear correlation, not HGR itself [1][7].
